Near Drowning

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
New medical breakthrough is saving the lives of children in near drowning incidents

Summary:
Dr Miles Bartlett has been featured in previous stories. he has since done a lot of work in Cardio Vascular systems- developing a system called AKMA whereby they place a “Third Lung”(artificial), which in turn gives the child’s lungs a chance to recover, This technique is also use in patients with respiratory problems/respiratory failure. In essence it is dialysis for the lungs and can be used to support the Cardio Vascular system. Dr Bartlett says they are the only paediatric unit doing it in South Africaa.

Further information:
They are battling to keep down the costs of performing such a procedure(it costs 1 million rand to perform it), but says in most cases medical aid covers it. His concern was that it was not affordable to average South Africans.

NEAR DROWNING – ECMO


V/O: Ten years ago Nash Kausiyo nearly drowned.

Gelfand: He just sneaked out and went to the pool, because everyone else had been playing at the pool. There was a ball in the pool and he wanted to grab it, and he tried to go for it and he fell. That was the beginning of a big story.

V/O: The 1 year-old toddler was under water for almost 10 minutes before he was found. A neighbor performed CPR before the paramedics arrived. His father Gelfand recalls what happened.

Gelfand: That paramedic happened to have Dr Bartlett”s number, and Dr Bartlett started giving instructions telephonically to the paramedic unit. We were told we needed to put an ice bed.

V/O: In 2005 Carte Blanche first met baby Nash and Dr Miles Bartlett, at Garden City Hospital. The pediatrician was pioneering the use of hypothermia to treat drowning victims. By dropping the temperature of the body with ice packs, they cooled the brain and managed to halt any further cell death. Little patients like baby Gabriel and baby Nash survived and managed to go home 3 weeks later with no long-term damage.

Gelfand: We had to teach him to walk again like a baby. The fortunate part he was only one year’s old. He had to redo everything that a child has to do, because he had forgotten. It was almost like a clean wiping of his memory as a result of being under water for that long.

V/O: Ironically Nash became a very good swimmer at the age of 3, even though he was told what had happened.

Nash: I was kind of shocked when I found out. But then I forgot about it. The past is the past, whatever happened, happened; so ja, that’s how I took it.

V/O: In 2010 Carte Blanche returned to Netcare Garden City Hospital to find the treatment for near drowning had changed slightly.

Dr Bartlett: We’re now using thermo-wrap, which is really a system that as you can see the child is wrapped in it. It has a box that pumps cold water in through the wrap, and we can control the temperature. So we measure core temperature and skin temperature and then our machine keeps our temperatures where we are.

V/O: But Dr Bartlett laments that all these cases are preventable, and with summer here again, parents are urged to be hyper-vigilant around water.

Dr Bartlett: If one looks at our statistics from 2006 we remain at an average of 35/40 drownings a year.

Devi: But you’re seeing a new trend now?

Dr Bartlett: We’ve noticed that we’ve started getting children drowning on school outings.

Devi: Older children?

Dr Bartlett: Six, seven-year-olds and I don’t know if the assumption is that these children can swim. I don’t know what the supervision is like when these children go on outings? But I think it’s very traumatic for a parent when you sign for your child to go on an outing and your child now gets admitted into an ICU having drowned.

Devi link: Since our last visit to the Paediatric ICU at Garden City Clinic there have been some changes. While the number of near drownings has remained constant, the treatment and technology has changed.

V/O: They now have an additional weapon in their arsenal. It’s called the ECMO machine, and this is the only registered paediatric ECMO centre in Africa.

Dr Bartlett: ECMO stands for Extra-Corporeal Membrane Oxygenation. Simplistically one can say it’s almost like dialysis for the lung. You’re oxygenating the blood and putting it back. In other words it’s like putting in a third lung temporarily. It’s not a permanent thing.

V/O: Ethan Smith and his twin brother have just turned one. Nathan recovered from a viral infection, but Ethan just got worse and was transferred to Garden City.

Dr Naidoo: Ethan was referred from another hospital, having been admitted there with severe respiratory distress. They identified an adeno viral pneumonia. And because he was deteriorating they transferred him across to Garden City.
He was not improving, in fact deteriorating quite quickly.
V/O: Dr Krubin Naidoo is a paediatric cardiac surgeon registered with the international ECMO Life Support Organization. When all the usual interventions weren’t helping it was decided to put Ethan on the ECMO machine. Dr Naidoo and his team performed the surgery in the ICU. A cannula was inserted into the jugular vein in Ethan’s neck that goes directly to his heart. Two lines were attached to carry blood from his body to the machine and back again.
Dr Naidoo: You can see the difference in the colour of his blood. The dark blood is extracted from the heart itself, extracted by this pump which spins to draw the blood out, and then pushes the blood out on this side and pushes it into the membrane lung. The membrane lung is attached to this oxygen supply here. In this you get gas exchange taking place: oxygen is delivered to the blood and carbon dioxide is removed, and then you can see the blood that exits it is much redder because that is the oxygenated blood. That blood then flows down and comes back up and that’s delivered into the patient.
V/O: Ethan is completely stable now, but heavily sedated so that he can’t move around.
Dr Naidoo: There are signs that his lungs are recovering, but that could take a long time. With this infection it could take up to 6 weeks.
Devi: So could he be on this ECMO machine for 6 weeks?
Dr Naidoo: He could be on this for 6 weeks.
Devi: If it wasn’t for this ECMO machine what would Ethan’s prognosis be?
Dr Naidoo: He most likely would have died.
Devi link: The ECMO machine may be saving lives, but it’s not cheap. It costs about R100 000 per day.

Dr Bartlett: If a child spends a week on that you’re looking at close to a million rand.

Devi: What do the medical aids say?

Dr Bartlett: We haven’t had a problem with them yet, quite surprisingly. They’ve been okay with it.

Devi: What does ECMO do for children that have been involved in a drowning?

Dr Bartlett: We’re struggling because we’ve got a child who’s drowned, the brain is compromised, but we’re battling with a heart that’s a bit dicey, we’re struggling with lungs that are not working properly and that can take us hours to try and rectify. So what the ECMO does is we can immediately take care of all of that. We can cool the child with ECMO, we can improve lung oxygenation, and we can improve blood pressure.

V/O: But the ECMO treatment is only used in extreme cases. It’s a multi-disciplinary intervention and carries substantial risk.

Dr Naidoo: This is an invasive form of therapy; there are numerous complications that can and do occur.
Devi: For example?
Dr Naidoo: Clotting of the circuit, bleeding of the patient, volume loss, you can get destruction of the blood cells, accumulation of fluid around the lungs, around the heart; even rupture of the heart itself.

V/O: Bur for Dr Bartlett the benefits outweigh the risks.

Dr Bartlett: In this unit it has made a huge difference. We don’t get children anymore that die in respiratory failure. So we’ll try the other modalities – but at least we know that if we fail it’s really a bridge to ECMO. If it works, wonderful we’ve avoided ECMO. If it doesn’t we can move on within 6 hours to ECMO.

Devi link: The ECMO machine is not a silver bullet. It’s a last resort. 25% of patients don’t make it – but the other 75% do.

V/O: In August this year 10 year-old Christiaan Nell suddenly developed respiratory distress.

Yolande: It was a Saturday we were still at home braaing and having fun, and Christiaan came to me and said that he cannot breathe.

V/O; His mother Yolande was surprised.

Yolande: On the Friday before he got sick he still actually did cross country running and he was fine.

V/O: After one night at N17 hospital in Springs, he was transferred to Garden City Hospital.

Yolande: We got to Garden City and Dr Bartlett saw him and said he’s going to put Christiaan on the ventilator, because at this stage Christiaan is not breathing on his own. He’s already on 100% oxygen and more than 100% they can’t give him.

Dr Bartlett: I euphemistically thought this is going to be a breeze; in 2 or 3 days we’ll have him out. The problem was he didn’t behave like an asthma, he wasn’t responding to therapy.

Yolande: They then picked up that Christiaan had like 4 viruses, and they basically festered in his heart and his lungs.

Dr Bartlett: He had adeno virus, which is what this little boy Ethan has got; he had meta pneumo virus, and bocca virus and rhino virus.

V/O: He decided to put Christiaan on the ECMO machine as nothing else was working.

Yolande: When they started off they said Christiaan – with the viruses and everything, and him not responding like they want him to – he’s going to be 6 weeks on the ECMO. And Christian was only 6 days on the ECMO. Christian went onto the ECMO on the Monday and on the Tuesday Dr Naidoo said this is a miracle, he can’t believe it.

Devi: So he spent 6 days on the ECMO machine?

Yolande: Six days on the ECMO machine, 23 days in hospital in total.

Devi: If there was no ECMO intervention, then?

Dr Bartlett: He wouldn’t have survived.

Devi: As clear-cut as that, Dr Bartlett?

Dr Bartlett: As clear-cut as that.

Devi: If you look at Christiaan you’d never know this happened to him a few months ago?

Yolande: Except for the miracle marks he’s got you wouldn’t know that he was very, very sick. I don’t think he knows how sick he was. In one way we’ve been blessed. We were truly, truly blessed.

Devi: Do you ever get used to this, saving children’s lives?

Dr Bartlett: It’s always been my passion – intensive care – to give good care to children. It really gives on a lot of joy to be able to return a child to a parent. You can imagine there’s nothing worse for a parent than losing a child. But we can really give it our best shot to do the best for that child that we can, with what we have.
